title: Antique Sees 17% Upside in Jio as Tariff Hike Holds the Key
excerpt: Antique Stock Broking argues a 15% sector tariff hike could unlock about Rs 190 per share and push Jio's ARPU toward Rs 300, valuing the IPO at about 15.6 times EV/EBITDA.
body:
• Antique Stock Broking sees 17% upside for Jio Platforms from its IPO valuation, rating the issue at about 15.6 times EV/EBITDA against Bharti Airtel as the main peer comparison.
  • The core of the call is tariffs: a 15% sector-wide hike could unlock about Rs 190 per share in value and push Jio's ARPU toward Rs 300, narrowing the gap with Airtel.
  • Antique also counts 2G-to-smartphone and JioBharat migration, plus enterprise and digital services, as recurring growth levers beyond the listing itself.
  • For investors, the distinction matters: this is a post-listing value call based on tariff execution, not a restatement of the IPO price band — if hikes slip, the upside case weakens.

Antique Stock Broking has put a 17% upside on Jio Platforms from its IPO valuation, in a brokerage call that turns less on the listing itself than on what happens to mobile tariffs afterwards. Moneycontrol reported the headline finding — that a 15% tariff hike could unlock about Rs 190 per share — and a summary of Antique's report carried by Whalesbook puts Jio's valuation at about 15.6 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, which the brokerage views as competitive against Bharti Airtel.

This article covers only that new analyst development. The Videshi's earlier coverage set out the IPO's scale and price band; Antique's note is a separate, forward-looking valuation argument published as the issue opened.

The Tariff Maths Behind the Call

Antique's central assumption is a sector-wide tariff increase of about 15%. In a market where Jio and Airtel together serve the large majority of mobile users, a coordinated industry hike flows largely to revenue rather than to subscriber churn, because customers have few equivalent alternatives. The brokerage argues that such a hike would lift average revenue per user toward Rs 300, narrowing Jio's current ARPU gap with Airtel, and that the incremental revenue carries high margins because the network cost base is already built.

That mechanism is why a tariff number, rather than subscriber growth, now drives most Jio valuation models. Other brokerages cited in Forbes India's IPO coverage make a similar point in different multiples: Geojit put the upper price band at 15 times FY26 EV/EBITDA on a post-issue basis, SBI Securities at 34.4 times FY26 earnings, and Canara Securities argued the multiple sits at the lower end versus peers. The estimates differ, but the shared driver is tariff-led ARPU expansion.

Migration and Enterprise as the Second Leg

Antique's second argument is migration. Millions of users in India remain on 2G networks, and Jio's budget JioBharat base is a pipeline of customers who can move to higher-value smartphone plans over time. Each migration raises ARPU without requiring a headline tariff change, giving the company a recurring growth source that is less politically sensitive than price hikes.

Beyond consumer mobile, the report points to Jio's fibre and tower infrastructure, low enterprise and small-business adoption of digital services, and a proprietary technology and patent portfolio that could be deployed internationally. Forbes India's coverage echoes that framing, with analysts at SBI Securities and Systematix citing home broadband, JioFiber and JioAirFiber growth, cloud and AI services, satellite connectivity and overseas deployment of Jio's platforms as the longer-term monetisation path. Jio reported 533.3 million customers and about 49.8% wireless broadband market share, with 284.9 million 5G customers.

Risks and What to Watch

Brokerage upside is not a guarantee, and Antique's case rests on execution outside Jio's full control. A tariff hike requires the whole sector, including Airtel and Vodafone Idea, to move, and it must survive regulatory and political scrutiny in a market where mobile prices are a household cost issue. Telecom also remains capital-intensive: continued 5G investment can pressure margins even as revenue rises.

The near-term markers are concrete. Watch whether a tariff announcement follows the listing, whether reported ARPU moves toward Rs 300 in subsequent quarters, and whether 2G and JioBharat migration shows up in subscriber mix. If tariffs stall, the 17% upside case loses its main engine and Jio trades on its digital-services optionality alone — a slower, harder-to-value story. If the hike lands, Antique's Rs 190-per-share unlock becomes the benchmark against which the stock's first year will be judged.
